title: BBC to cut raft of Radio 4 programmes including You and Yours
content:
The BBC has announced it will be cutting a raft of Radio 4 programmes including the long-running consumer and social affairs show You and Yours.
The social sciences show Thinking Allowed will also be cut along with arts and ideas programme Free Thinking, as the corporation seeks £500m savings.
Other shows such The Artificial Human and Open Country will also go, it was announced on Thursday, while Radio 5 Live will also see a reduction in commissioning on its schedule and podcasts.
The BBC has committed to investing in a new consumer programme, though, and two new weekly shows exploring ideas shaping the world, and the impact of technology and AI.
Radio 4's flagship history, science and culture show, In Our Time, will expand in length, as will Start the Week and Farming Today.
Director of BBC Sounds Jonathan Wall said they were "reshaping BBC speech audio" in order to "build a strong future for trusted journalism, distinctive storytelling and programmes that bring people together".
"By commissioning fewer programmes overall, we can focus our investment and make our best shows work across broadcast, on demand and different formats," he said in a statement.
"That means accelerating growth on our own digital platforms and reaching more people beyond the BBC, while maintaining the strength of Radio 4 and 5 Live, the country's two biggest speech radio stations."
He added that the "difficult decisions" about cuts to shows and staff were "not based on cost alone", saying: "We need to make significant savings while investing for the future."
Last month, director general Matt Brittin said the BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services.
Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever".
In June, the BBC announced 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage in its plan to save £500m across the corporation over the next two years.
Staff were told of proposals including ending Radio 4's The World Tonight, and reducing the number of permanent presenters on Today from five to four, with a single anchor on Saturdays.
It was revealed that BBC One's Breakfast would no longer be shown on Sunday mornings, and that the production teams making Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg and Newsnight would merge.
It followed April's announcement that the BBC would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - or almost one in 10 - in an attempt to tackle "significant financial pressures".
Last week, an influential group of MPs said the BBC licence fee should be extended to cover services other than TV, and that the corporation's charter review should be scrapped and made permanent.
In its recommendations, the DCMS committee also said that political appointments to the BBC board should end, to improve public trust.
The BBC's Samira Hussain explains the impact the $110bn merger will have on consumers of both entertainment giants.
The merger of two of Hollywood's biggest movie studios comes after months of legal disputes and concern over competition.
The gala is leaving traditional US broadcast networks for live worldwide streaming.

title: How boxing inspired a play about men's mental health
content:
For many athletes, years of training can provide a routine, a purpose and an identity - but what happens when it all stops?
That question is at the heart of a new play which explores men's mental health through the world of boxing.
The Corner Man follows a fighter forced to confront life outside the ring after spending years dedicated to the sport.
Through his story, the play explores losing a sense of purpose, the difficulty some men have talking about their mental health and the support they can find in each other.
Writer and producer Cathal J Ferris said the idea grew from his own experience of boxing and conversations with fighters.
"What is a boxer after he retires really played on my mind," he said, adding that the same questions around identity and purpose can apply beyond sport.
The play follows Liam Casey, who has dedicated much of his life to boxing, from the age of about nine into his 30s.
For Ferris, the story is not only about leaving the ring, but about losing the routine that comes with it.
"The idea of structure and what life is like whenever you lose that structure definitely played on my mind," he said.
"There are people who work in jobs for 10, 12, 13-odd years and just decide to change industries.
"I think there's a lot of people who may not know what to do with themselves after."
Ferris grew up performing in amateur theatre in Belfast and Lisburn before going to drama school in London in 2012.
He said returning home had given him the chance to tell new stories about the place where he grew up.
"I'm a Belfast boy at heart, and it is great to tell stories from the city," he said.
Ferris said "the boxing community in Belfast is phenomenal" and that it played an important part in shaping the story.
Alongside boxing, the play also looks at how men talk - or sometimes do not talk - about their mental health.
"I think the old phrase is 'say nothing', and we know that all too well," Ferris said.
"As a man, it is definitely hard for myself to talk about these things, and I try to be a little bit more open."
In the play, Liam struggles with life after boxing, but it is the other men around him who help provide a support network - something Ferris said was an important part of the story.
"It is healthy to talk, so definitely if you're a man and you're struggling, at least speak to somebody," he said.

title: Gaten Matarazzo on life after Stranger Things as he makes West End debut
content:
Keeping your balance on a revolving stage probably sounds easy when you compare it with battling demogorgons, but Gaten Matarazzo points out one big difference.
You don't get the luxury of "thirty takes" to get it right in front of a live audience.
The former Stranger Things star's currently playing Mark in a modern revival of rock musical Rent on London's West End.
He tells BBC Newsbeat that having a proper schedule and remembering to stay hydrated makes a "refreshing change" from filming the Netflix smash-hit that made him famous.
Matarazzo shot to fame in 2016 as endearing super-geek Dustin Henderson - a role he calls "the greatest honour of his life".
The saga finally concluded last December after five seasons, and there's been interest in what the show's cast will do next.
"It's something you do inevitably step away from," says Matarazzo
"We finished filming in 2024 - there's no more show to film."
"I still love what I do very much, I want to keep on doing it."
Casting big names from TV and film in theatre shows is a growing trend, and one that sometimes provokes accusations of cashing in .
But Matarazzo has plenty of stage experience, having performed on Broadway when he was a child.
He says the time commitment involved meant it was impossible to "blend both worlds".
"My favourite part of theatre specifically is the schedule," he says.
"Going to bed at the same time and waking up at the same time.
"I've always thrived under a schedule and when I don't have one I feel insane."
In Rent, Matarazzo plays struggling film-maker Mark, who chronicles and narrates the lives of his friends.
It has been 30 years since the show first opened off-Broadway in New York, but the actor says there are "certain songs that weirdly resonate now".
"What You Own, which feels like a reflection on information overload, is incredibly relevant," he says.
"That's really fun to sing in context of today."
When it was first performed, Rent shone a light on young friends and artists living in late 1980s and early 1990s New York during the HIV/Aids crisis.
